title: Which way to the tree is shorter?
description: A tent, a tree and a pole mark the corners of a plot, and the straight path from the tent to the tree is compared with the path through the pole. Keeko doubts the result and says the path through the pole is shorter because each of its parts is short.
teaching_notes: One idea: the straight path between two places is shorter than the path that goes through a third place. Watch for children who compare one part of the roundabout path with the direct path and forget to add both parts.

source: Which path is shorter: the straight path from the tent to the tree, or the path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree?
video_script.why: The child has seen arcs that fail to meet and now looks for the reason in the lengths of paths between three places.
video_script.substitution: The straight path from the tent to the tree is thirty metres, and the path through the pole is twenty metres plus twenty five metres.
video_script.anchor: A plot with a tent, a tree and a pole at its three corners
video_script.wrong_answer: the path through the pole is shorter
video_script.wrong_move: A child sees that each part of the path through the pole is shorter than the direct path and forgets that both parts must be walked.
video_script.payoff_line: The direct path of thirty metres is shorter than the roundabout path of forty five metres.

final_answer.spoken: the direct path of thirty metres is shorter than the roundabout path of forty five metres

hold_back: The direct path of 30 m is shorter
never_show: the verdict that the direct path is shorter before the answer beat
maths_rules: direct path tent to tree = 30 m
roundabout path tent to pole to tree = 20 + 25 = 45 m
30 < 45, so the direct path is shorter
the same holds for every pair of the three corners
video_script.design: One idea: the direct path between two places is shorter than the roundabout path through a third. A plot with three corners, two paths in two colours; Keeko's doubt closes the video.
open_questions: The path lengths of 30, 20 and 25 metres come from the worklist; the book text shows the plot without printing any length.

<bookmark mark='fix'/>Together they make forty five metres, which is more than thirty.
